q: What is the maximum item size in DynamoDB?

exp.a: 256 KB is not the correct maximum item size for DynamoDB.
exp.b: The maximum item size in DynamoDB is 400 KB, including attribute names and values.
exp.c: 1 MB exceeds DynamoDB's maximum item size limit.
exp.d: 64 KB is too small; DynamoDB allows items up to 400 KB.

q: How many Local Secondary Indexes (LSIs) can you create per DynamoDB table?

exp.a: 3 is incorrect; DynamoDB allows more LSIs per table.
exp.b: You can create a maximum of 5 Local Secondary Indexes per DynamoDB table.
exp.c: 10 is incorrect; the limit is 5 LSIs per table.
exp.d: 20 is the limit for Global Secondary Indexes, not LSIs.

q: How many Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) can you create per DynamoDB table by default?

exp.a: 5 is the limit for Local Secondary Indexes, not GSIs.
exp.b: 10 is incorrect; DynamoDB allows more GSIs.
exp.c: You can create up to 20 Global Secondary Indexes per DynamoDB table by default.
exp.d: GSIs are not unlimited; the default limit is 20 per table.

q: What does one Read Capacity Unit (RCU) represent for strongly consistent reads in DynamoDB?

opts.a: One read per second for items up to 2 KB
opts.b: One read per second for items up to 4 KB
opts.c: Two reads per second for items up to 4 KB
opts.d: One read per second for items up to 8 KB

exp.a: 2 KB is incorrect; one RCU covers items up to 4 KB for strongly consistent reads.
exp.b: One RCU provides one strongly consistent read per second for items up to 4 KB in size.
exp.c: Two reads per second for 4 KB items describes eventually consistent reads (1 RCU = 2 eventually consistent reads).
exp.d: 8 KB is incorrect; one RCU handles items up to 4 KB for strongly consistent reads.

q: What does one Write Capacity Unit (WCU) represent in DynamoDB?

opts.a: One write per second for items up to 1 KB
opts.b: One write per second for items up to 2 KB
opts.c: One write per second for items up to 4 KB
opts.d: Two writes per second for items up to 1 KB

exp.a: One WCU provides one write per second for items up to 1 KB in size.
exp.b: 2 KB is incorrect; one WCU handles writes up to 1 KB.
exp.c: 4 KB applies to read capacity units, not write capacity units.
exp.d: One WCU provides only one write per second, not two.

q: How many eventually consistent reads per second does one RCU provide for items up to 4 KB?

exp.a: 1 read per second is for strongly consistent reads, not eventually consistent.
exp.b: One RCU provides 2 eventually consistent reads per second for items up to 4 KB.
exp.c: 4 is incorrect; the correct number is 2 eventually consistent reads per RCU.
exp.d: 8 is incorrect; one RCU supports only 2 eventually consistent reads per second.

q: What is the maximum length of a DynamoDB partition key value?

exp.a: 256 bytes is too small; DynamoDB allows larger partition key values.
exp.b: 1024 bytes is the maximum for sort key values, not partition key values.
exp.c: The maximum length of a partition key value in DynamoDB is 2048 bytes.
exp.d: 4096 bytes exceeds the DynamoDB partition key value limit.

q: What is the maximum length of a DynamoDB sort key value?

exp.a: 256 bytes is too small for the sort key value limit.
exp.b: The maximum length of a sort key value in DynamoDB is 1024 bytes.
exp.c: 2048 bytes is the limit for partition key values, not sort key values.
exp.d: 4096 bytes exceeds the DynamoDB sort key value limit.

q: How long are DynamoDB Streams records retained?

exp.a: 12 hours is too short; DynamoDB Streams retains records longer.
exp.b: DynamoDB Streams records are retained for 24 hours.
exp.c: 48 hours exceeds the retention period for DynamoDB Streams.
exp.d: 7 days is the retention for Kinesis Data Streams (default), not DynamoDB Streams.

q: How many days of backup history does DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) provide?

exp.a: 7 days is incorrect; PITR provides a longer recovery window.
exp.b: 14 days is incorrect; PITR provides more than 14 days.
exp.c: 30 days is incorrect; the correct duration is 35 days.
exp.d: DynamoDB PITR allows you to restore your table to any point in time within the last 35 days.

q: What is the maximum data stored per partition in DynamoDB?

exp.a: 5 GB is incorrect; DynamoDB allows more data per partition.
exp.b: Each partition in DynamoDB can hold up to 10 GB of data.
exp.c: 20 GB exceeds the per-partition storage limit.
exp.d: 50 GB exceeds the per-partition storage limit.

q: What is the maximum throughput per partition in DynamoDB?

exp.a: 1000 RCU and 500 WCU is incorrect; partitions support higher throughput.
exp.b: Each DynamoDB partition supports up to 3000 RCU and 1000 WCU.
exp.c: 5000 RCU and 2000 WCU exceeds the per-partition limit.
exp.d: 10000 RCU and 5000 WCU far exceeds the per-partition limit.

q: How many items can you retrieve in a single BatchGetItem request?

exp.a: 25 is the limit for BatchWriteItem, not BatchGetItem.
exp.b: 50 is incorrect; BatchGetItem allows more items.
exp.c: A single BatchGetItem request can retrieve up to 100 items across multiple tables, up to 16 MB total.
exp.d: 500 exceeds the BatchGetItem limit.

q: How many items can you write in a single BatchWriteItem request?

exp.a: 10 is incorrect; BatchWriteItem supports more items.
exp.b: A single BatchWriteItem request can write (put or delete) up to 25 items across multiple tables, up to 16 MB total.
exp.c: 50 exceeds the BatchWriteItem limit.
exp.d: 100 is the limit for BatchGetItem, not BatchWriteItem.

q: How many items can a single DynamoDB transaction include?

exp.a: 10 is incorrect; DynamoDB transactions can include more items.
exp.b: 25 is the limit for BatchWriteItem, not transactions.
exp.c: 50 is incorrect; transactions support up to 100 items.
exp.d: A single DynamoDB transaction can include up to 100 unique items or up to 4 MB of data.

q: How much additional capacity do DynamoDB transactional reads consume compared to standard reads?

exp.a: Transactional reads consume more capacity than standard reads.
exp.b: Transactional reads consume 2x the read capacity of a standard strongly consistent read.
exp.c: 3x is incorrect; transactional reads consume 2x capacity.
exp.d: 4x is incorrect; transactional reads consume 2x capacity.

q: How much additional capacity do DynamoDB transactional writes consume compared to standard writes?

exp.a: Transactional writes consume more capacity than standard writes.
exp.b: Transactional writes consume 2x the write capacity of a standard write.
exp.c: 3x is incorrect; transactional writes consume 2x capacity.
exp.d: 4x is incorrect; transactional writes consume 2x capacity.

q: What is the maximum number of tables you can create per AWS account per region by default?

exp.a: 25 is incorrect; DynamoDB allows many more tables per region.
exp.b: 256 is the initial default in some older documentation, but the current default is 2500.
exp.c: The default limit is 2500 tables per AWS account per region (can be increased via support request).
exp.d: There is a limit, though it can be increased by contacting AWS support.

q: What is the SLA uptime commitment for DynamoDB single-region tables?

exp.a: 99.9% is lower than DynamoDB's SLA commitment.
exp.b: 99.95% is lower than DynamoDB's SLA.
exp.c: DynamoDB offers 99.99% availability SLA for single-region tables.
exp.d: 99.999% applies to DynamoDB Global Tables, not standard single-region tables.

q: What SLA does DynamoDB Global Tables provide?

exp.a: 99.9% is too low for Global Tables SLA.
exp.b: 99.99% is the SLA for single-region DynamoDB tables.
exp.c: DynamoDB Global Tables provides a 99.999% (five nines) availability SLA.
exp.d: No AWS service guarantees 100% availability.

q: If you need to read an item of 10 KB with strong consistency, how many RCUs are consumed?

exp.a: 2 RCU would only cover 8 KB for strongly consistent reads (2 × 4 KB).
exp.b: 10 KB / 4 KB = 2.5, rounded up to 3 RCUs for a strongly consistent read.
exp.c: 4 RCU would be more than needed; 10 KB needs only 3 RCUs.
exp.d: 10 RCU is far more than needed for a 10 KB item.

q: If you need to write an item of 3 KB, how many WCUs are consumed?

exp.a: 1 WCU only covers 1 KB of write data.
exp.b: 2 WCU only covers 2 KB of write data.
exp.c: 3 KB / 1 KB = 3 WCUs consumed for writing a 3 KB item.
exp.d: 4 WCU is more than needed for a 3 KB item.

q: If you need to read an item of 8 KB with eventual consistency, how many RCUs are consumed?

exp.a: 0.5 RCU is not a valid RCU consumption value in this context.
exp.b: 8 KB / 4 KB = 2 (for strongly consistent), but eventually consistent reads use half the capacity, so 2 / 2 = 1 RCU.
exp.c: 2 RCU would be needed for strongly consistent reads of 8 KB, not eventually consistent.
exp.d: 4 RCU is far more than needed for an 8 KB eventually consistent read.

q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a DynamoDB DAX cluster?

exp.a: 5 nodes is below the maximum DAX cluster size.
exp.b: 10 nodes is below the maximum DAX cluster size.
exp.c: A DynamoDB DAX cluster can have a maximum of 11 nodes (1 primary + 10 read replicas).
exp.d: 15 exceeds the maximum DAX cluster node count.

q: What is the default TTL for items in the DAX item cache?

exp.a: 1 minute is not the default DAX item cache TTL.
exp.b: The default TTL for the DAX item cache is 5 minutes.
exp.c: 10 minutes is not the default DAX item cache TTL.
exp.d: 30 minutes is not the default DAX item cache TTL.

q: How many DynamoDB Streams view types are available?

exp.a: 2 is incorrect; there are more view types available.
exp.b: 3 is incorrect; there are 4 stream view types.
exp.c: There are 4 stream view types: KEYS_ONLY, NEW_IMAGE, OLD_IMAGE, and NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES.
exp.d: 5 is incorrect; DynamoDB Streams has exactly 4 view types.

q: How much storage cost savings does DynamoDB Standard-IA provide compared to Standard?

exp.a: 30% is less than the actual savings offered by Standard-IA.
exp.b: DynamoDB Standard-IA offers up to 60% lower storage costs compared to the Standard table class.
exp.c: 80% exceeds the actual savings offered by Standard-IA.
exp.d: 90% exceeds the actual savings offered by Standard-IA.

q: What is the maximum number of projected attributes in a DynamoDB secondary index (INCLUDE type)?

exp.a: 10 is incorrect; more attributes can be projected.
exp.b: 20 is the number of GSIs allowed, not projected attributes.
exp.c: You can project up to 100 non-key attributes into a secondary index when using INCLUDE projection type.
exp.d: There is a limit of 100 non-key projected attributes (when using INCLUDE).

q: What is the maximum size of data returned by a single BatchGetItem call?

exp.a: 1 MB is the limit for a single Query or Scan call, not BatchGetItem.
exp.b: 4 MB is the size limit for transactions, not BatchGetItem.
exp.c: A single BatchGetItem call can return up to 16 MB of data.
exp.d: 64 MB exceeds the BatchGetItem data limit.

q: What is the maximum total data size for a DynamoDB transaction (TransactWriteItems or TransactGetItems)?

exp.a: 1 MB is the limit for Query/Scan results, not transactions.
exp.b: DynamoDB transactions are limited to 4 MB of data in total across all items in the transaction.
exp.c: 16 MB is the limit for BatchGetItem, not transactions.
exp.d: 25 MB is not a DynamoDB limit.

q: How often can you switch between DynamoDB provisioned and on-demand capacity modes?

exp.a: Once per day is close but not the precise AWS term.
exp.b: You can switch between provisioned and on-demand capacity modes once every 24 hours.
exp.c: Switching is not unlimited; there is a 24-hour cooldown.
exp.d: Once per week is incorrect; you can switch every 24 hours.

q: What is the maximum discount available with DynamoDB reserved capacity (3-year term)?

exp.a: 50% is less than the maximum available discount.
exp.b: 60% is less than the maximum available discount.
exp.c: DynamoDB reserved capacity offers up to 77% savings with a 3-year term compared to on-demand pricing.
exp.d: 90% exceeds the maximum discount available for DynamoDB reserved capacity.

q: What is the maximum retention period when using Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB?

exp.a: 24 hours is the DynamoDB Streams retention, not Kinesis Data Streams.
exp.b: 7 days is the default Kinesis retention, but extended retention is available.
exp.c: 30 days is less than the maximum available retention.
exp.d: Kinesis Data Streams supports up to 365 days of data retention.

q: What is the maximum number of attributes that can be defined as key schema elements for a DynamoDB table?

exp.a: 1 attribute is for a simple primary key (partition key only), but composite keys use 2.
exp.b: A DynamoDB table key schema can have at most 2 attributes: one partition key and one optional sort key.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not support 3 key attributes in the table schema.
exp.d: 5 attributes cannot be part of the table's key schema.

q: What is the maximum nesting depth for DynamoDB document types (Maps and Lists)?

exp.a: 8 levels is below the actual maximum nesting depth.
exp.b: 16 levels is below the actual maximum nesting depth.
exp.c: DynamoDB supports a maximum nesting depth of 32 levels for document type attributes.
exp.d: 64 levels exceeds the DynamoDB nesting limit.

q: What is the maximum number of concurrent DynamoDB Streams consumers for a single shard?

exp.a: More than 1 consumer can read from a DynamoDB stream shard simultaneously.
exp.b: A DynamoDB stream shard supports a maximum of 2 simultaneous readers/consumers to avoid throttling.
exp.c: 5 simultaneous readers would exceed the shard read capacity.
exp.d: There is a limit of 2 concurrent readers per shard.

q: What is the maximum batch size (number of records) that Lambda can receive from DynamoDB Streams in a single invocation?

exp.a: 100 is the default batch size, but not the maximum.
exp.b: 1,000 is below the maximum configurable batch size.
exp.c: The maximum batch size for Lambda reading from DynamoDB Streams is 10,000 records per invocation.
exp.d: 100,000 exceeds the maximum batch size limit.

q: A company has a DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity of 100 RCUs. They need to perform 100 strongly consistent reads per second on items that are 8 KB each. What will happen?

opts.a: All reads will succeed without throttling
opts.b: Reads will be throttled because 200 RCUs are needed
opts.c: Reads will be throttled because 400 RCUs are needed

exp.a: 100 RCUs is insufficient for 8 KB strongly consistent reads at 100 per second.
exp.b: 8 KB / 4 KB = 2 RCUs per read. 100 reads × 2 RCUs = 200 RCUs needed. With only 100 provisioned, requests will be throttled.
exp.c: 400 RCUs would be needed for 4 RCUs per read, which is not the case for 8 KB items.
exp.d: In provisioned mode without Auto Scaling enabled, DynamoDB does not automatically increase capacity.

q: An application performs 500 eventually consistent reads per second on items of 3.5 KB each. How many RCUs should be provisioned?

exp.a: 125 RCU is half of what's needed.
exp.b: 3.5 KB rounds up to 4 KB = 1 RCU per strongly consistent read. Eventually consistent reads cost half: 0.5 RCU per read. 500 × 0.5 = 250 RCUs.
exp.c: 500 RCU would be for strongly consistent reads of 4 KB items.
exp.d: 1000 RCU is far more than needed for this scenario.

q: You need to calculate the RCUs required for 50 strongly consistent reads per second, with each item being 6 KB. How many RCUs do you need?

exp.a: 50 RCU would only cover items up to 4 KB each.
exp.b: 75 RCU is incorrect; the calculation yields a different result.
exp.c: 6 KB / 4 KB = 1.5, rounded up to 2 RCUs per read. 50 reads × 2 RCU = 100 RCUs.
exp.d: 150 RCU is more than needed for this scenario.

q: You need 80 eventually consistent reads per second for items of 12 KB each. How many RCUs are required?

exp.a: 80 RCU does not account for the item size exceeding 4 KB.
exp.b: 12 KB / 4 KB = 3 RCUs for strongly consistent. For eventually consistent: 3 / 2 = 1.5 RCU per read. 80 × 1.5 = 120 RCUs.
exp.c: 160 RCU would be for strongly consistent reads, not eventually consistent.
exp.d: 240 RCU is double what is needed.

q: You need 100 writes per second for items of 2.5 KB each. How many WCUs are required?

exp.a: 100 WCU only covers 1 KB items.
exp.b: 200 WCU is insufficient for 2.5 KB items.
exp.c: 250 WCU is incorrect; 2.5 KB rounds up to 3 KB.
exp.d: 2.5 KB rounds up to 3 KB. 3 KB / 1 KB = 3 WCUs per write. 100 × 3 = 300 WCUs.

q: You need 200 transactional writes per second for items of 2 KB each. How many WCUs are required?

exp.a: 200 WCU does not account for item size or transactional overhead.
exp.b: 400 WCU only accounts for item size (2 WCU per item) but not transactional overhead.
exp.c: 600 WCU is incorrect.
exp.d: 2 KB / 1 KB = 2 WCUs per write. Transactional writes cost 2x, so 2 × 2 = 4 WCUs per transactional write. 200 × 4 = 800 WCUs.

q: What is the WCU cost of a transactional write for a 1.5 KB item?

exp.a: 1 WCU doesn't account for rounding up or transactional overhead.
exp.b: 2 WCU accounts for item size (1.5 rounds to 2) but not transactional overhead.
exp.c: 3 WCU is incorrect.
exp.d: 1.5 KB rounds up to 2 KB = 2 WCUs. Transactional writes cost 2x, so 2 × 2 = 4 WCUs.

q: What is the RCU cost of a transactional read for a 6 KB item?

exp.a: 2 RCU is the cost for a strongly consistent read of 6 KB, not transactional.
exp.b: 3 RCU is incorrect.
exp.c: 6 KB / 4 KB = 1.5, rounded up to 2 RCUs for strongly consistent. Transactional reads cost 2x, so 2 × 2 = 4 RCUs.
exp.d: 6 RCU is more than needed for a transactional read of 6 KB.

q: You need to perform 30 transactional reads per second on items of 8 KB each. How many RCUs are required?

exp.a: 60 RCU doesn't account for the transactional overhead.
exp.b: 8 KB / 4 KB = 2 RCUs per strongly consistent read. Transactional = 2 × 2 = 4 RCUs per read. 30 × 4 = 120 RCUs.
exp.c: 240 RCU would be for 60 transactional reads, not 30.
exp.d: 480 RCU is far more than needed.

q: A DynamoDB table uses On-Demand capacity. What is the initial throughput for a newly created table?

exp.a: On-demand is not unlimited from the start; it has initial limits that scale up.
exp.b: 40,000 is the account-level default limit, not the initial table throughput.
exp.c: A new on-demand table can handle up to 4,000 RCUs and 4,000 WCUs immediately. It scales up as traffic increases.
exp.d: 100 is too low; newly created on-demand tables support higher initial throughput.

q: What is the maximum previous peak that DynamoDB On-Demand mode can instantly accommodate?

opts.b: Up to double the previous peak

exp.a: On-demand can handle more than just the previous peak.
exp.b: DynamoDB On-Demand can instantly accommodate up to double (2x) the previous peak traffic. Beyond that, throttling may occur until capacity scales further.
exp.c: 5x exceeds the instant scaling capability.
exp.d: 10x exceeds the instant scaling capability.

q: How long does DynamoDB retain burst capacity from unused provisioned throughput?

exp.a: 1 minute is too short for burst capacity retention.
exp.b: DynamoDB retains up to 5 minutes (300 seconds) of unused provisioned capacity for occasional traffic bursts.
exp.c: 30 minutes exceeds the burst capacity retention period.
exp.d: 1 hour exceeds the burst capacity retention period.
